section: Exercise 10 — No difference, or cannot tell? [Apply]
text:
Exercise 10 — No difference, or cannot tell? [Apply]
Run the t-test on enjoyment by build and on items_collected by build. Neither is significant. For which one can you say there is no meaningful difference, and for which can you only say we cannot tell?






TipSolution






enjoy <- t.test(enjoyment ~ build, data = sessions)
items <- t.test(items_collected ~ build, data = sessions)

enjoy$conf.int

[1] -0.3483742  0.3483742
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95

items$conf.int

[1] -1.0061446  0.3394779
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95

tapply(sessions$items_collected, sessions$build, mean)

       A        B 
4.016667 4.350000 


Read each interval against the size of the variable. Enjoyment’s interval runs from -0.35 to 0.35 on a seven-point scale: whatever the true difference is, it is too small to matter. That is no meaningful difference. The items interval runs from -1.01 to 0.34 items, when a typical player collects about 4. Build B’s players could be collecting up to 1.0 more items each, or up to 0.3 fewer. That is cannot tell.



Write 2 sentences: why is “not significant” a weaker statement than “the confidence interval is narrow and sits around zero”?

title: Lab 02 — Comparing Builds
section: Exercise 11 — “Players play longer in Build B” [Decide]
text:
Exercise 11 — “Players play longer in Build B” [Decide]
t.test(session_minutes ~ build) gives p = 0.037, and Build B’s sessions are about 3 minutes longer on average. The producer wants to put “players play 3 minutes longer in Build B” in the pitch. Do you let them? Test before you decide: compare session length between the builds for players who did not quit in frustration.






TipSolution






not_frustrated <- sessions[sessions$quit_reason != "Frustrated", ]
t.test(session_minutes ~ build, data = not_frustrated)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  session_minutes by build
t = 0.63783, df = 88.126, p-value = 0.5252
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group A and group B is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -1.564143  3.042780
sample estimates:
mean in group A mean in group B 
       26.19750        25.45818 

frustrated <- sessions[sessions$quit_reason == "Frustrated", ]
tapply(frustrated$session_minutes, frustrated$build, median)

   A    B 
11.7 11.7 


One defensible answer: no, because the claim describes the wrong thing. Among players who did not quit in frustration, Build A averaged 26.2 minutes and Build B 25.5 (p = 0.53). Frustration quits end at a median of about 11.7 minutes in both builds. Build B does not make anyone play longer. It makes fewer people quit early, and that pulls its average up. The honest pitch line is “fewer players quit in frustration”, which is also the stronger claim.
What makes it defensible. It checks what is driving the difference before describing it, and it replaces the claim with one the data supports.
What would make it indefensible. Approving the line because the p-value is below 0.05. The difference is real; the explanation attached to it is not.



Write 3 sentences: a significant difference in a mean can come from every player shifting a little or from a few players shifting a lot. How do you tell which, and why does it change the design conclusion?

title: Lab 02 — Comparing Builds
section: Exercise 12 — Which number goes in the report? [Decide]
text:
Exercise 12 — Which number goes in the report? [Decide]
You have three estimates of how much the signposting reduced wrong turns: the session-level test from Exercise 08, the paired study from Exercise 09, and a player-level test that averages each player’s 4 sessions first. Run the player-level test, then decide which result leads the report.






TipSolution






per_player <- aggregate(wrong_turns ~ player_id + build, data = sessions, FUN = mean)
player_test <- t.test(wrong_turns ~ build, data = per_player)

player_test$conf.int

[1] 2.361153 4.438847
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95

result$conf.int

[1] 2.480141 4.319859
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95

paired_test$conf.int

[1] 1.838014 3.695319
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95


One defensible answer: lead with the player-level result, and cite the paired study as support. The session-level test treats 120 sessions as independent when they come from 30 players, so its interval is narrower than the data justifies. The player-level interval, 2.4 to 4.4 wrong turns, is honest about that. The paired study, a different design with different players, points the same way, which is worth more than any single p-value.
What makes it defensible. It picks the analysis whose assumptions match how the data was collected, and it uses the other two as corroboration rather than choosing between them.
What would make it indefensible. Picking whichever result has the smallest p-value or the largest effect. That is choosing the answer, not the analysis.



Write 2 sentences: why is agreement between two differently designed studies stronger evidence than a very small p-value from one?

library(readr)

library(ggplot2)

sessions <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_sessions.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

Step 2. Add a geometry

ggplot(sessions, aes(x = wrong_turns)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1)








Pause here. Ask: this is correct. Why does it not answer “did Build B help”?
Step 3. Map a group, and watch it mislead

# fill = build inside aes() is a MAPPING: colour follows the data, legend appears.
# But histograms stack by default, so Build A floats on top of Build B.
ggplot(sessions, aes(x = wrong_turns, fill = build)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1)








Step 4. Facet instead, and label it for a reader

# fill = "grey60" OUTSIDE aes() is SETTING: fixed colour, no legend needed.
ggplot(sessions, aes(x = wrong_turns)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "grey60", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ build, ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "Wrong turns per session, by build",
       x = "Wrong turns", y = "Sessions")








Pause here. Ask: Build B is lower. What else is different about its shape?
Step 5. The mapping bug, on purpose

  geom_point(aes(colour = "blue"))








Step 6. The scatterplot, done properly

ggplot(sessions, aes(x = awareness, y = score)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey40") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black") +
  labs(title = "Awareness against score", x = "Awareness rating", y = "Score")

[1] 0.5907852

[1] 0.05307857

[1] -0.6562375

  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Mobility rating", y = "Survivability rating", colour = "Archetype")

Step 10. The t-test: size, interval, p-value

# Different players on each build, so the independent-samples test.
result <- t.test(wrong_turns ~ build, data = sessions)
result

95 percent confidence interval:

mean in group A mean in group B

[1] 2.480141 4.319859

[1] 0.95

Step 11. Same players, both builds

paired <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_paired.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Paired: each player compared with themselves, so player skill cancels out.
t.test(paired$wrong_turns_a, paired$wrong_turns_b, paired = TRUE)$conf.int

[1] 1.838014 3.695319
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95

# Same data, wrongly treated as two separate groups: a much wider interval.
t.test(paired$wrong_turns_a, paired$wrong_turns_b)$conf.int

[1] 1.180570 4.352763
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95


Step 12. Significant is not the same as important

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
text:
These are the questions that come up in the week after a playtest. None of them is exotic. All of them are painful to answer with a spreadsheet, and each one is answered below by a single figure and a few dozen lines of R.



The question you are actually asking
Answered by




I have 120 rows of results and no idea what is in them. Where do I start?
View 1


All four characters average about the same score. Does that mean they are balanced?
View 2


I designed four classes to play differently. Did they stay different once real people played them?
View 3


I want players to score higher. Which ability is actually worth buffing?
View 4


Testers keep giving up partway through. When do I lose them, and is it the same moment every time?
View 5


The survey came back with 960 ratings across eight questions. Which complaint do I fix first?
View 6


My frame-rate counter says 60 FPS. My testers say the game stutters. Who is lying?
View 7


How can I find where players are loitering, sniping, or being funnelled into a kill zone?
View 8


Which parts of my level is nobody using?
View 8


How did one particular player move through the level — did they learn the route, or wander?
View 8b



Every one of these is a question about your own game, asked of data your own engine can already record. The only thing missing is the ability to read it.

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
text:
Before you read any code
This document is a showcase, not a lesson. Nothing here is examinable and you are not expected to understand the code yet. Its only job is to show you what three weeks of R can do to a pile of raw playtest numbers.
Every figure below was produced from 5 CSV files, in chunks of between 11 and 61 lines of code. By the end of these notes you will be able to answer the first seven questions with base R, dplyr and ggplot2, producing plainer, static versions of the plots shown here. The three movement questions in View 8 use position data that stays in this showcase. The polish on this page is the destination, not the syllabus.






NoteThe data



Tidebreak is a fictional four-player top-down arena, used here so that the example is self-contained. The playtest recorded four things:








File
One row per
Holds




tidebreak_sessions.csv
player, per session
Six end-of-match ability ratings, eleven match statistics, session length and quit reason, for 120 sessions


tidebreak_survey.csv
player, per session
Eight agreement items rated 1 to 5


tidebreak_frame_times.csv
rendered frame
Frame time in milliseconds, by build and level zone


tidebreak_positions.csv
player, per second
Top-down position for eight players across one 180-second match



All four are synthetic, but they behave like the real thing: the numbers are messy, the interesting findings are not the obvious ones, and at least two widely held assumptions about the game turn out to be wrong.




Show the code
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)
library(DT)

sessions    <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_sessions.csv")
survey      <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_survey.csv")
frame_times <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_frame_times.csv")
positions   <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_positions.csv")
level       <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_level.csv")

# A small, fixed palette used by every figure in this document.
pal <- c(blue = "#2a78d6", orange = "#eb6834", aqua = "#1baf7a", yellow = "#eda100")
ink <- c(primary = "#0b0b0b", secondary = "#52514e", grid = "#e6e5e1")

# Each archetype keeps the same colour in every figure, so that a colour always
# means the same thing no matter which chart you are looking at.
arch_pal <- c(Scout = pal[["blue"]],  Sentinel = pal[["orange"]],
              Engineer = pal[["aqua"]], Duelist = pal[["yellow"]])

# Likewise for the two builds, which appear in Views 5 and 7.
build_pal <- c(A = pal[["orange"]], B = pal[["blue"]])

theme_tb <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold", colour = ink["primary"], size = 13),
      plot.subtitle   = element_text(colour = ink["secondary"], size = 11),
      axis.title      = element_text(colour = ink["secondary"], size = 10),
      axis.text       = element_text(colour = ink["secondary"]),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = ink["grid"], linewidth = 0.3),
      legend.position = "none"
    )
}

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
section: View 1 — The table you can actually read
text:
View 1 — The table you can actually read
Question: what happened in each session?
Before you analyse anything you need to be able to look at your data. A raw CSV in Excel is awkward at 120 rows and unusable at 120,000. A rendered table is searchable and sortable, and it goes straight into a report.
Sort by Score, or type Sentinel into the search box, and you will already see the finding that View 2 makes formal.


Show the code
sessions %>%
  select(Session = session_id, Player = player_id, Cohort = cohort,
         Archetype = archetype, Build = build, Score = score,
         Kills = kills, Deaths = deaths, `Alive (s)` = time_alive_s,
         Awareness = awareness) %>%
  datatable(
    rownames = FALSE,
    options  = list(pageLength = 8, dom = "ftip", scrollX = TRUE),
    caption  = "Tidebreak playtest: 120 sessions"
  ) %>%
  formatStyle("Score",
    background = styleColorBar(range(sessions$score), "#cde2fb"),
    backgroundSize = "98% 60%", backgroundRepeat = "no-repeat",
    backgroundPosition = "center")

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
text:
View 2 — Distributions, not averages
Question: which archetype performs best?
The tempting answer is to compare four average scores. Do that here and the archetypes look almost identical, which would be a design decision made on a misreading.
A violin plot draws the whole distribution. Read the Sentinel shape: it is not one hump but two. Sentinel runs either anchor the objective and score well, or collapse in the opening seconds and score badly. There is almost no middle. That is a balance problem an average would have hidden completely.


Show the code
sessions %>%
  mutate(archetype = fct_reorder(archetype, score, .fun = median)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(archetype, score, fill = archetype)) +
  geom_violin(colour = NA, alpha = 0.85, width = 0.9) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, fill = "white", colour = ink[["secondary"]],
               outlier.shape = NA, linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = arch_pal) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title    = "Sentinel is bimodal: it either anchors the round or dies in it",
    subtitle = "Score distribution by archetype, 30 sessions each. Box shows median and interquartile range.",
    x = NULL, y = "Score"
  ) +
  theme_tb()

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
section: View 3 — Six numbers as a shape
text:
View 3 — Six numbers as a shape
Question: are the four archetypes actually playing differently?
Each session ends with six ability ratings on a 0–100 scale. Comparing four archetypes across six measures means twenty-four numbers, which no one can hold in their head. Drawn as a radar, each archetype becomes a shape you can recognise at a glance, and the grey outline behind each one is the all-player average for reference.
The shapes are distinct and they are roughly the shapes the design intended. That is the result you want from this chart: confirmation that the archetypes are not quietly converging on the same playstyle.


Show the code
metrics <- c("accuracy", "mobility", "survivability",
             "objective_control", "support", "awareness")

pretty <- c(accuracy = "Accuracy", mobility = "Mobility",
            survivability = "Survival", objective_control = "Objective",
            support = "Support", awareness = "Awareness")

long <- sessions %>%
  select(archetype, all_of(metrics)) %>%
  pivot_longer(-archetype, names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(metric = factor(pretty[metric], levels = unname(pretty)))

by_arch <- long %>% group_by(archetype, metric) %>% summarise(value = mean(value))
overall <- long %>% group_by(metric) %>% summarise(value = mean(value))

ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = overall, aes(metric, value, group = 1),
               fill = NA, colour = ink[["grid"]], linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_polygon(data = by_arch,
               aes(metric, value, group = archetype, fill = archetype, colour = archetype),
               alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = by_arch, aes(metric, value, colour = archetype), size = 1.8) +
  coord_polar(clip = "off") +
  facet_wrap(~archetype, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = arch_pal) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = arch_pal) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100), breaks = c(25, 50, 75)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Four archetypes, four distinct ability profiles",
    subtitle = "Mean end-of-match rating per ability. Grey outline is the all-player average.",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_tb() +
  theme(axis.text.y   = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x   = element_text(size = 7),
        strip.text    = element_text(face = "bold", colour = ink[["primary"]]),
        panel.spacing = unit(1.6, "lines"),
        plot.margin   = margin(10, 20, 10, 20))

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
text:
View 4 — What actually drives score
Question: which abilities and behaviours move the scoreboard?
A correlogram puts every pair of variables in one picture. Blue means the two rise together, red means one rises as the other falls, and pale means no relationship at all.
Three things to read off it:

Awareness is the strongest positive correlate of score. Map knowledge beats mechanical skill in this build.
Shots fired is essentially uncorrelated with score. Players who shoot more do not win more, which contradicts what the team assumed.
Mobility and survivability pull against each other, which is the intended trade-off working as designed.



Show the code
vars <- c("accuracy", "mobility", "survivability", "objective_control",
          "support", "awareness", "shots_fired", "distance_m",
          "kills", "deaths", "objectives", "score")

nice <- c(accuracy = "Accuracy", mobility = "Mobility", survivability = "Survival",
          objective_control = "Objective ctrl", support = "Support",
          awareness = "Awareness", shots_fired = "Shots fired",
          distance_m = "Distance", kills = "Kills", deaths = "Deaths",
          objectives = "Objectives", score = "Score")

cm <- cor(sessions[vars])
ord <- hclust(as.dist(1 - cm))$order
lv  <- nice[vars[ord]]

cm_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(cm)) %>%
  setNames(c("a", "b", "r")) %>%
  mutate(a = factor(nice[as.character(a)], levels = lv),
         b = factor(nice[as.character(b)], levels = lv)) %>%
  filter(as.integer(a) < as.integer(b))   # lower triangle only; the diagonal is always 1

ggplot(cm_long, aes(a, b, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", r),
                colour = abs(r) > 0.55), size = 2.9) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#e34948", mid = "#f0efec", high = "#2a78d6",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1), name = "r") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "white", `FALSE` = ink[["secondary"]]),
                      guide = "none") +
  coord_fixed() +
  labs(
    title    = "Awareness drives score; shots fired does not",
    subtitle = "Pearson correlation between every pair of measures, 120 sessions.",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_tb() +
  theme(axis.text.x       = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        legend.position   = "right",
        panel.grid.major  = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor  = element_blank())

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
text:
View 5 — When people stop playing
Question: we changed how the game explains its objective. Did it keep anyone?
A retention curve shows what fraction of participants were still playing at each minute of the test. It is the shape that matters, not the endpoint: a smooth decay means people drifted away, a cliff means something specific pushed them out.
Build A has a cliff. Between minutes 11 and 13 it drops from 88% to 68%, and 15 of the 17 people who left in that window are logged as frustration quits. Build B, which explains its objective differently, is still at 90% at minute 13 and loses five people to frustration across the whole test against Build A’s twenty.
Now look at what a summary table would have told you: median session length is 23.2 minutes for Build A and 27.1 for Build B. That reads as a modest improvement. The curve shows something else — one specific, fixable moment where a fifth of the Build A testers gave up.


Show the code
minutes <- seq(0, 32, by = 0.25)

retention <- map_dfr(c("A", "B"), function(b) {
  lengths <- sessions %>% filter(build == b) %>% pull(session_minutes)
  tibble(build = b, minute = minutes,
         pct = map_dbl(minutes, ~ 100 * mean(lengths >= .x)))
})

ends <- retention %>% group_by(build) %>% slice_max(minute, n = 1)

ggplot(retention, aes(minute, pct, colour = build)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 11, xmax = 13, ymin = 0, ymax = 100,
           fill = ink[["grid"]], alpha = 0.55) +
  annotate("text", x = 13.4, y = 24, hjust = 0, size = 3.2,
           colour = ink[["secondary"]],
           label = "88% to 68% in two minutes,\nalmost all frustration quits") +
  geom_step(linewidth = 1.1, direction = "hv") +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = paste0("Build ", build)),
            hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.6, size = 3.6, fontface = "bold",
            show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = build_pal) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 37), breaks = seq(0, 30, 5),
                     labels = function(x) paste0(x, " min")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100), labels = function(y) paste0(y, "%")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Build A loses people at a cliff; Build B does not",
    subtitle = "Percentage of participants still playing, by minute of the test session.",
    x = NULL, y = "Still playing"
  ) +
  theme_tb()

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
section: View 6 — What players said, ranked by how badly it went
text:
View 6 — What players said, ranked by how badly it went
Question: the survey has eight questions and 120 responses. Which one should we act on first?
Eight averages tell you almost nothing, because a mean of 3.0 can mean everyone was indifferent or that half loved it and half hated it. A diverging bar chart splits each item at the neutral response: disagreement runs left, agreement runs right, and the items sort by the net.
The result is uncomfortable in the way real survey results usually are. The art is the best-rated thing in the game by a distance. The worst-rated item is whether players ever knew what they were supposed to be doing — the same thing that drives the cliff in View 5. People praise the visuals and quit over the design.


Show the code
item_label <- c(
  objective_clear     = "I always knew what my objective was",
  death_understood    = "I understood why I died",
  difficulty_fair     = "The difficulty felt fair",
  level_navigable     = "The level was easy to navigate",
  would_play_again    = "I would play this again",
  match_length        = "The match length felt right",
  controls_responsive = "The controls felt responsive",
  visual_style        = "The visual style is appealing"
)

resp_label <- c("Strongly disagree", "Disagree", "Neutral", "Agree", "Strongly agree")

props <- survey %>%
  pivot_longer(-session_id, names_to = "item", values_to = "resp") %>%
  count(item, resp) %>%
  complete(item, resp = 1:5, fill = list(n = 0)) %>%
  group_by(item) %>% mutate(pct = 100 * n / sum(n)) %>% ungroup()

# Net agreement decides the order; the neutral block is split so the bars
# pivot on a true zero rather than on the left edge.
ranking <- props %>%
  group_by(item) %>%
  summarise(net = sum(pct[resp >= 4]) - sum(pct[resp <= 2])) %>%
  arrange(net)

item_levels <- unname(item_label[ranking$item])

as_bars <- function(d, sign) {
  d %>%
    mutate(signed = sign * if_else(resp == 3, pct / 2, pct),
           item   = factor(unname(item_label[item]), levels = item_levels),
           resp   = factor(resp_label[resp], levels = resp_label))
}

# The two sides stack in opposite directions, so that the strongest opinion
# always sits furthest from the centre line.
bars_neg <- props %>% filter(resp <= 3) %>% as_bars(-1)
bars_pos <- props %>% filter(resp >= 3) %>% as_bars(+1)

ranking <- ranking %>%
  mutate(item = factor(unname(item_label[item]), levels = item_levels))

ggplot(mapping = aes(signed, item, fill = resp)) +
  geom_col(data = bars_neg, width = 0.72, position = position_stack()) +
  geom_col(data = bars_pos, width = 0.72, position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#fcfcfb", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_text(data = ranking, aes(x = 106, y = item, label = sprintf("%+.0f", net)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3.3, fontface = "bold",
            colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Strongly disagree" = "#e34948",
                               "Disagree"          = "#f2a9a8",
                               "Neutral"           = "#d9d8d4",
                               "Agree"             = "#9ec5f4",
                               "Strongly agree"    = "#2a78d6")) +
  # coord_cartesian zooms; scale limits would DROP the segments that fall
  # outside them, silently truncating the longest bars.
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-60, 90, 30),
                     labels = function(x) paste0(abs(x), "%")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-68, 112)) +
  labs(
    title    = "They love the art and cannot tell what the game wants",
    subtitle = "Share of 120 responses. Bars pivot on neutral; the number is net agreement.",
    x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_tb() +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        legend.text     = element_text(size = 9),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
section: View 7 — The frame-rate counter is lying to you
text:
View 7 — The frame-rate counter is lying to you
Question: both builds average about 59 FPS. Testers say Build B stutters. Who is right?
Both are. Average frame rate is a mean, and a mean is exactly the wrong summary for a quantity where the rare bad values are the entire user experience. Build B renders almost every frame slightly faster than Build A. It also renders one frame in every twenty-five — about twice a second — in 35 to 55 ms instead of 17, and only in one zone of the level: the corridor that View 8 identifies as the choke point.
The trace shows it. The table shows why the FPS readout missed it: the two builds are separated by 0.05 ms at the mean and by 20 ms at the 99th percentile.


Show the code
ggplot(frame_times %>% filter(zone == "Corridor", frame <= 400),
       aes(frame, ms, colour = build)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1000 / 60, linetype = "22",
             colour = ink[["secondary"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.45) +
  facet_wrap(~build, ncol = 1, labeller = labeller(build = function(b) paste("Build", b))) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = build_pal) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 60), breaks = c(1000/60, 30, 45, 60),
                     labels = c("16.7\n(60 FPS)", "30", "45", "60")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Identical average, one of them unplayable",
    subtitle = "Frame time in the Corridor zone, first 400 frames. Dashed line is the 60 FPS budget.",
    x = "Frame", y = "Frame time (ms)"
  ) +
  theme_tb() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", colour = ink[["primary"]]))

frame_times %>%
  group_by(Build = build) %>%

    `Worst (ms)`   = round(max(ms), 1)

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
text:
View 8 — Where players actually stand
Question: where are the choke points, the camping spots and the dead space?
This is the figure that changes level layouts. The blue field is total time spent per square metre across the whole match. The moving dots are the eight players, one frame per second, coloured by whether they are moving, loitering or holding position. Dark blocks are cover; the block in the north-east is the raised gantry.
Press play, or drag the slider.
Three readings, all of them actionable:

The gap between the central core and the east block carries almost all lateral traffic, and 14 of the 20 deaths in this match happened inside it. That is a choke point.
Two players spend the entire match holding the north-east gantry. Long dwell, no movement, high kill share: a sniper perch.
The west corner is never visited by anyone. That is floor space the level is paying for and not using.



Show the code
# Time spent per 2m x 2m cell, for the background field.
gx_seq <- seq(1, 59, 2)
gy_seq <- seq(1, 39, 2)

field <- positions %>%
  mutate(gx = floor(x / 2) * 2 + 1, gy = floor(y / 2) * 2 + 1) %>%
  count(gx, gy) %>%
  complete(gx = gx_seq, gy = gy_seq, fill = list(n = 0)) %>%
  arrange(gy, gx)

z <- matrix(field$n, nrow = length(gy_seq), ncol = length(gx_seq), byrow = TRUE)

# Level geometry drawn as rectangles behind the data.
shapes <- pmap(level, function(block, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, kind) {
  list(type = "rect", x0 = xmin, x1 = xmax, y0 = ymin, y1 = ymax,
       fillcolor = if (kind == "elevated") "#6f6e6a" else "#2f2e2c",
       # The gantry is walkable, so it stays translucent and the dwell field
       # underneath it still reads.
       opacity = if (kind == "elevated") 0.35 else 0.92,
       line = list(width = 0), layer = "above")
})

# The animated layer starts at the first second where all three states occur, so
# that the legend is complete from the first frame.
first_full <- positions %>%
  group_by(t) %>% summarise(k = n_distinct(state)) %>%
  filter(k == 3) %>% slice_min(t) %>% pull(t)

deaths <- positions %>% filter(event == "death")

text:
Exercise 06 — Faster players are more fragile? [Decide]
The balance designer reads Exercise 05 and proposes a patch: “Faster players are more fragile, so when a Scout player gets faster, cut their health to match.” Redraw the scatterplot with each archetype in its own colour and its own trend line, then decide whether the patch follows from the data.






TipSolution






ggplot(sessions, aes(x = mobility, y = survivability, colour = archetype)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Mobility against survivability, by archetype",
       x = "Mobility rating", y = "Survivability rating", colour = "Archetype")







sessions |>
  group_by(archetype) |>
  summarise(r = cor(mobility, survivability))

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  archetype     r
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 Duelist   0.302
2 Engineer  0.512
3 Scout     0.465
4 Sentinel  0.598


One defensible answer: no, the patch reads the data backwards. Across all players the correlation is -0.66. Within every archetype it is positive, from 0.3 to 0.6. The downward trend is the gap between archetypes: Scouts are built fast and fragile, Sentinels slow and tough. Within any one archetype, better players are better at both. Archetype is the confounding variable: it drives both measures, and ignoring it reverses the direction of the relationship.
What makes it defensible. It checks the relationship inside the groups the design is made of before drawing a conclusion about individuals, and it says what the overall correlation does show: the archetypes are balanced against each other as intended.
What would make it indefensible. Applying the patch because the correlation is strong. A strong correlation across groups says nothing about what happens to one player within a group.



Write 3 sentences: name the confound, say what it does to the conclusion, and say which part of the report this belongs in.

Exercise 09 — “Without reducing enjoyment” [Decide]
The research question has two halves. Test the second: did Build B reduce enjoyment? Use enjoyment from sessions (1–7) and would_play_again from the survey, and decide what the report may claim.






TipSolution

enjoy$estimate

mean in group A mean in group B 
       3.933333        3.933333 

enjoy$conf.int

[1] -0.3483742  0.3483742
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95

agree_by_build[agree_by_build$item == "would_play_again", ]

1 would_play_again   0.5 0.517 0.0167


One defensible answer: the report may claim no meaningful reduction. Mean enjoyment was 3.93 in Build A and 3.93 in Build B. Exercise 11 — Limitations and the conclusion [Decide]
Write parts 8 and 9 of the report. Part 8 lists what could make your conclusion wrong. Part 9 is one finding in What → Pattern → Meaning → Action form that answers the research question; a finding that does not name an action is not finished (rule 10). Every number is inline R.

wt$estimate

mean in group A mean in group B 
       8.916667        5.516667 

wt$conf.int

  Novice  18 15

  Veteran 16 18


One defensible part 8.

Each of the 30 players contributed 4 sessions, so the 120 sessions are not independent, and the session-level test is more confident than the data justifies.
Every measure was taken after one session. Nothing here shows whether the difference lasts.
Cohorts were not perfectly balanced between the builds; the cohort table is in the report so the reader can judge.
Comments record how a session felt, and do not agree with the wrong-turn counts (see the Challenge).
Strong correlations in this data can reverse within archetypes (Exercise 06), so no relationship here is reported as a cause without checking within groups.

One defensible part 9.

What. Wrong turns per session in 120 sessions, and enjoyment on a seven-point scale, compared between Build A and Build B.
Pattern. Build B players averaged 5.5 wrong turns against Build A’s 8.9, a reduction of between 2.5 and 4.3 per session at 95% confidence. Enjoyment was unchanged, with a mean of 3.93 in both builds.
Meaning. The guidance works, and costs nothing players noticed.
Action. Keep Build B’s guidance and carry it into the next build. Retest with an on-screen objective added, since objective clarity was the item that moved most.

What makes it defensible. Part 8 names limitations specific to this data, not a generic “the sample was small”. Part 9’s Action follows from its Meaning, and its Pattern gives a size and an interval.

A terminal keeps the environment it started with, and VS Code hands every new terminal a cached copy. So after installing anything, a brand new terminal panel will still not see it.

title: Comparing Playtest Conditions
text: Week 2, second cycle, for everyone, before Part B of Lab 02. It takes the question every A/B playtest ends with, “is Build B better?”, and splits it into the two questions it actually contains: would the difference hold up with other players, and is it big enough to act on? The worked example is the one to remember: two results that are both statistically significant, one of which you should act on and one of which you should not.

title: Comparing Playtest Conditions
Comparing Playtest Conditions
text:
Why This Matters for Playtesting
Every build comparison ends with a difference. Build B’s players took fewer wrong turns, or scored more, or quit less. The difference is always there, because two groups of people never produce identical numbers. The question is never “is there a difference?” but “is this difference telling me something about the build, or only about the players who happened to turn up?”
A playtest is a sample. The 30 people who played Tidebreak stand in for everyone who will play it after launch. Run the test again next week with different players and every number would move. Before you rebuild a level on the strength of a difference, you need to know whether that difference would survive a second playtest.
And a real difference can still be worthless. With enough data, a change too small for any player to notice becomes statistically detectable. A result can be certain and irrelevant at the same time. Deciding whether it matters is a design judgement, and no test makes it for you.

title: Comparing Playtest Conditions
text:
The Workflow
Comparing two conditions always follows the same six steps, in this order:

visualise → describe → estimate difference → confidence interval → statistical test → interpret









Step
Question
Tool




Visualise
What do the two distributions look like?
Side-by-side boxplots or faceted histograms


Describe
Where is each centre, how wide is each spread?
Medians, means, IQRs, standard deviations


Estimate difference
How far apart are the groups in this sample?
Difference in means


Confidence interval
How far apart could they plausibly be, for players in general?
t.test()


Statistical test
Could a gap this size be chance alone?
t.test()


Interpret
Is it real, is it big enough, and what do we do?
Judgement



The test comes fifth, not first. A p-value with no picture and no size attached cannot be interpreted. If the boxplots show a gap nobody would care about, no p-value changes that (rule 7).

title: Comparing Playtest Conditions
text:
Sampling Variability
Sampling variability is the fact that a different sample gives different numbers, even when nothing about the game has changed. Some of the difference between two groups is the build. Some of it is which players ended up in which group: a few more veterans in one, a bad night’s sleep in the other.
To see it, pretend the Tidebreak team could only afford 15 sessions per build, and draw six such playtests at random from the sessions they actually have. The difference in mean wrong turns comes out as 3.9, 4.5, 2.4, 3.0, 4.9, 2.6. Same builds, same kind of player, six different answers.
Smaller samples swing further. The fewer players you test, the more one unusual player moves the result (rule 8). The statistics in the rest of these notes exist to put a size on that swing.

title: Comparing Playtest Conditions
text:
Estimates and Confidence Intervals
The observed difference is the gap between the groups in your sample: Build A’s mean minus Build B’s. It is your best single guess at the true difference, and it is almost certainly not exactly right.
A confidence interval is a range of plausible values for the true difference, given the sample. A 95% confidence interval is built by a method that captures the true value in 95% of the playtests you could have run.
Read the interval as a range of sizes. “Build B’s players took 2.5 to 4.3 fewer wrong turns” tells a designer both that the effect is real and how big it might be. An interval that runs from almost nothing to something large says the direction is clear and the size is not.
Width is information. A narrow interval means the sample pins the difference down. A wide one means more players are needed before the size can be trusted. More players, or less variation between them, narrows it.
If the interval includes zero, “no difference” is still plausible. That is the link between confidence intervals and the test that follows.

title: Comparing Playtest Conditions
text:
Hypothesis Testing
A hypothesis test asks one narrow question: if the builds really made no difference, how surprising would this data be?
The null hypothesis is the claim of no difference: Build A and Build B produce the same mean number of wrong turns. The alternative hypothesis is that they do not. The test looks for evidence against the null.
The p-value is the probability of seeing a difference at least as large as the one observed, if the null hypothesis were true. A small p-value means the data would be surprising in a world where the builds did not differ.






Important



A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
It is calculated by assuming the null is true, so it cannot also measure how likely the null is. p = 0.03 does not mean “a 3% chance the builds are the same”. It means “if the builds were the same, a gap this large would turn up about 3% of the time”.


Statistical significance means the p-value fell below a threshold chosen before looking, conventionally 0.05. It means “unlikely to be chance alone” and nothing more. Choose the threshold in advance for the same reason you decide what would change your mind before looking at the data (rule 1).
Not significant does not mean no difference. A large p-value means this sample could not rule out chance. That can be because there is no difference, or because there were too few players to see one. The confidence interval tells you which.

title: Comparing Playtest Conditions
text:
Statistical and Practical Significance
Practical significance is whether a difference is large enough to change a design decision. Statistical significance cannot tell you this, because it depends on how much data you have as well as on how big the difference is.
The Tidebreak frame-time capture has 3000 frames from the Atrium zone. In the Atrium, Build B’s frames are 0.42 ms faster than Build A’s, p < 0.001. That is about as statistically significant as a result gets, and a player would need to perceive a difference of less than half a millisecond per frame to notice it. Nobody should schedule work around it.









Practically small
Practically large




Statistically significant
Real but not worth acting on
Act on it


Not significant
Nothing to see, if the interval is narrow
Test more players: the sample was too small to tell



Always report the size of the difference. “Significant” alone hides which row of that table you are in.

title: Comparing Playtest Conditions
text:
Two Designs: Independent and Paired
How the playtest was run decides which test you use.
Independent samples. Different players test each build. That is how the Tidebreak sessions file was collected: 30 players, each of whom played only one build. The comparison is between two separate groups of people, so differences between the people are mixed in with differences between the builds. Use the independent-samples t-test:
t.test(wrong_turns ~ build, data = sessions)
Paired. The same players test both builds. tidebreak_paired.csv records a second study in which 30 players each played both builds. Each player is compared with themselves, so their skill cancels out. Use the paired t-test:
t.test(paired$wrong_turns_a, paired$wrong_turns_b, paired = TRUE)
Player ability is the biggest source of variation in most playtests. A confident player takes few wrong turns in any build; a lost one takes many in any build. In the paired data, a player’s wrong turns in Build A and in Build B have a correlation of 0.67: the same people do well or badly in both. The paired design removes that variation, which is why it can detect a difference with far fewer players.
Paired designs bring their own problems. A player who plays both builds plays the second one with more experience (learning effects), in a fixed position (order effects) and more tired (fatigue effects). If everyone plays Build A first, some of Build B’s improvement is just practice. The fix is to give half the players Build A first and half Build B first. tidebreak_paired.csv does not record which build each player played first, so this study cannot rule it out.

title: Comparing Playtest Conditions
text:
Assumptions, Practically
A t-test is reliable when these hold closely enough. None needs a formal test; each needs a look.









Assumption
What it means
How to check
Tidebreak




Independence
One observation does not influence another
Think about how the data was collected
Each player contributed 4 sessions, so the 120 sessions are really 30 players


No strong outliers
No few values dominate the means
Boxplots
3 flagged wrong-turn counts across 120 sessions


Approximate normality
Each group roughly bell-shaped
A Q-Q plot
Close enough; counts are whole numbers, which shows as steps


Appropriate design
Independent test for separate groups, paired test for the same people
How the playtest was run
Sessions: independent. Paired file: paired



With a few dozen players per group, the normality assumption matters least. The t-test tolerates moderate departures. Strong outliers and a mismatched design matter far more, and no amount of data fixes the wrong design.
The independence problem has a simple check. Average each player’s four sessions into one value, then compare players rather than sessions. If the conclusion survives, the repeated sessions were not driving it. The R Demonstrations below do exactly that.

title: Comparing Playtest Conditions
text:
Worked Examples
Did the signposting reduce wrong turns? The six steps, in order.
Visualise.

ggplot(sessions, aes(x = build, y = wrong_turns)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey85") +
  labs(title = "Wrong turns per session, by build", x = "Build", y = "Wrong turns")








Build B’s box sits lower and is taller. The boxplot flags 3 outlying sessions in Build A and 0 in Build B, too few to dominate either mean.
Describe. Build A’s median is 9 wrong turns and Build B’s is 5. Build B’s spread is wider: an IQR of 4.25 against 2.
Estimate the difference. Build A’s players averaged 8.9 wrong turns and Build B’s 5.5: a difference of 3.4.
Confidence interval. The 95% interval for the difference runs from 2.5 to 4.3 wrong turns. It is nowhere near zero.
Test. p < 0.001. If the builds made no difference, a gap this size would almost never occur.
Interpret. The signposting reduced wrong turns, and the smallest plausible reduction, 2.5 per session, is still large enough for a player to feel. This is a result to act on: keep the signposting.
Was Build B harder? The same six steps on the 1–7 difficulty rating give a second significant result. Build B was rated 0.42 points harder, p = 0.032, with a confidence interval from 0.04 to 0.8 points.
Three things say not to act on it. The size is small: under half a point on a seven-point scale. The interval’s lower end, 0.04, is a difference no player would report. And the play data does not back it up: deaths did not differ between the builds (p = 0.679). Statistically significant, practically marginal, and unsupported by what players actually did. Note it, and check it in the next playtest.

R Demonstrations

library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

sessions <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_sessions.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
paired   <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_paired.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)


tapply(sessions$wrong_turns, sessions$build, mean)

       A        B 
8.916667 5.516667 

tapply(sessions$wrong_turns, sessions$build, sd)

       A        B 
2.374238 2.702740 


Describe before testing. These are the numbers the test will compare.

result <- t.test(wrong_turns ~ build, data = sessions)
result


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  wrong_turns by build
t = 7.3208, df = 116.07, p-value = 3.492e-11
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group A and group B is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 2.480141 4.319859
sample estimates:
mean in group A mean in group B 
       8.916667        5.516667 


t.test(y ~ group) is the independent-samples t-test. R runs the Welch version by default, which does not assume the two builds have the same spread, and that is the right default. Read three lines of the output: the sample estimates (the two means), the 95 percent confidence interval (for Build A minus Build B) and the p-value.

result$estimate

mean in group A mean in group B 
       8.916667        5.516667 

result$conf.int

[1] 2.480141 4.319859
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95

result$p.value

[1] 3.491687e-11


$ pulls single parts out of the result, which is how you get numbers into a sentence with inline R instead of copying them by hand.

t.test(paired$wrong_turns_a, paired$wrong_turns_b, paired = TRUE)


    Paired t-test

data:  paired$wrong_turns_a and paired$wrong_turns_b
t = 6.0932, df = 29, p-value = 1.234e-06
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 1.838014 3.695319
sample estimates:
mean difference 
       2.766667 


paired = TRUE compares each player’s two values. The estimate is the mean difference: on average, a player took 2.8 fewer wrong turns in Build B than in Build A.

t.test(paired$wrong_turns_a, paired$wrong_turns_b)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  paired$wrong_turns_a and paired$wrong_turns_b
t = 3.4918, df = 57.85, p-value = 0.0009258
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 1.180570 4.352763
sample estimates:
mean of x mean of y 
 9.366667  6.600000 


The same data tested as if the players were different people. The estimate is the same, but the interval is 3.2 wrong turns wide against 1.9 for the paired test. Ignoring the pairing throws away what the design bought you.

paired$improvement <- paired$wrong_turns_a - paired$wrong_turns_b

ggplot(paired, aes(x = improvement)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "grey60", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Wrong turns saved per player, Build A minus Build B",
       x = "Improvement (wrong turns)", y = "Players")








For paired data, draw the differences. 26 of 30 players took fewer wrong turns in Build B, 2 took the same number and 2 took more. geom_vline() marks zero, the line between better and worse.

ggplot(sessions, aes(sample = wrong_turns)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ build)








A Q-Q plot places each value against where it would sit if the data were perfectly normal. Points close to the line mean close to normal. Here both builds follow it through the middle, in horizontal steps because wrong turns are whole numbers. Build A’s lowest few points drop away below the line: those are the 3 sessions its boxplot flagged, players who barely got lost at all. A handful of points bending off at one end is close enough for a t-test with 60 sessions per build. A whole curve bending away from the line would not be.

per_player <- aggregate(wrong_turns ~ player_id + build,
                        data = sessions, FUN = mean)
nrow(per_player)

[1] 30

t.test(wrong_turns ~ build, data = per_player)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  wrong_turns by build
t = 6.7116, df = 27.324, p-value = 3.125e-07
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group A and group B is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 2.361153 4.438847
sample estimates:
mean in group A mean in group B 
       8.916667        5.516667 


The independence check. aggregate() averages each player’s sessions into one row, leaving 30 players instead of 120 sessions. The difference is the same and the interval is a little wider, from 2.4 to 4.4, because there are fewer independent observations. The conclusion survives.

title: Comparing Playtest Conditions
text:
Interpretation Guidance
What the data shows. In this playtest, Build B’s players averaged 3.4 fewer wrong turns per session than Build A’s (95% CI 2.5 to 4.3, p < 0.001). In a separate study where 30 players played both builds, they took 2.8 fewer in Build B (95% CI 1.8 to 3.7).
What the analysis suggests. The signposting helps players find their way, and by enough to matter. Two different designs, with different players, point the same way.
What can legitimately be concluded. The reduction is very unlikely to be chance, and even its smallest plausible size is a noticeable improvement. The paired study cannot separate the signposting from practice, because play order was not recorded; the independent study does not have that problem, which is why the two together are stronger than either alone.
Write the result as a sentence a designer can use. Lead with the size, give the interval, then the p-value:

Build B’s players took 3.4 fewer wrong turns per session on average (95% CI 2.5 to 4.3, p < 0.001).

“The result was significant” is not a finding. It names no size and no action (rule 10).

title: Comparing Playtest Conditions
text:
Common Mistakes
Reading the p-value as the chance the null is true. It is the chance of data this extreme if the null is true. The two are different, and only the first one is what R reports.
Reading “not significant” as “no difference”. It means this sample could not tell. Check the confidence interval: narrow and around zero is evidence of no meaningful difference; wide is a sample too small to say.
Reading “significant” as “important”. The Atrium frame times are among the most significant results in the whole playtest and among the least important.
Testing before looking. A t-test on data you have not drawn can hide outliers, skew or two groups mixed together. Visualise first, every time.
Using the independent test on paired data. It ignores what the pairing bought you and gives an interval far wider than the data supports. Match the test to the design.
Testing every column and reporting what came up. At a 0.05 threshold, roughly one test in twenty on builds that do not differ will come up significant anyway. Decide which comparisons answer your question before you run any of them.
Counting sessions as players. Four sessions from one player are not four independent players. Check that the result survives when each player counts once.

title: Comparing Playtest Conditions
text:
Summary

A playtest is a sample. Another group of players would give different numbers, so every difference needs a measure of how far it could swing.
Work in order: visualise, describe, estimate the difference, compute the confidence interval, test, interpret.
A confidence interval gives a range of plausible sizes. Report it with every difference.
A p-value is how surprising the data would be if there were no difference. It is not the probability that there is no difference.
Statistically significant means unlikely to be chance. Practically significant means big enough to act on. You need both.
Different players on each build: independent-samples t-test. The same players on both: paired t-test, with the play order varied.
The signposting reduced wrong turns by 3.4 per session, and the smallest plausible reduction is still worth having.

title: Comparing Playtest Conditions
text:
Reflective Questions

Build B’s difficulty rating was significantly higher, but deaths did not change. What would you need to see in the next playtest to take the difficulty result seriously?
A colleague says the paired study proves the signposting works because its p-value is smaller. What is wrong with that argument, and what does the paired study add that the sessions data does not?
You can afford 30 testers for the next build comparison. Would you run them as two independent groups of 15 or as one paired group of 30? What would you have to control in the paired design?
A producer asks, “is it significant?”. What do you tell them instead, and why is that a more useful answer?

title: Distributions and Variation
Distributions and Variation
Distributions and Variation
text:
Why This Matters for Playtesting
Every design question is really a question about players, plural, and players differ. A level that takes eight minutes on average can be a level everyone finishes in eight minutes, or a level half the testers finish in four and the other half abandon. Those are different games with different fixes, and the average cannot tell them apart.
The players you design for are rarely the average player. The ones who quit, the ones who get stuck, the ones whose machine stutters: they live in the edges of the distribution, and the edges are exactly what a mean averages away.
Variation is information, not noise. When two builds differ in how spread out their players are, that difference is often the finding. A build that tightens the spread has made the experience more consistent, even if the average has not moved.

title: Distributions and Variation
text:
Variation Between Players
The variation in a variable is how much its values differ from one another. Some of it is the game: a harder route produces more deaths. Some of it is the player: skill, experience and patience vary before anyone touches your build. You cannot remove the second kind, so you have to measure it.
The standard deviation is the typical distance of a value from the mean. A small standard deviation means players cluster tightly around the average; a large one means the average is a poor guide to any individual. It is in the same units as the data, so a standard deviation of 3 ms on a frame time is directly comparable to the 16.7 ms a 60 FPS frame is allowed.
Standard deviation belongs to the mean. It measures distance from the mean, so it inherits the mean’s weakness: a few extreme values inflate it. For skewed data, the interquartile range from the previous notes is the better description of spread.

title: Distributions and Variation
text:
Distributions and Skew
A distribution is the full pattern of values: which ones occur, and how often. A histogram draws it. Every summary statistic is an attempt to describe a distribution in one number, and every one of them fails for some distribution.
Skew is a distribution leaning to one side. A right skew has a long tail of large values: most frames are quick, a few are very slow. A left skew has a long tail of small values: most players stay for the full session, a few leave early. The mean is pulled towards the tail; the median is not. That is why the gap between them tells you which way the data leans.
Game data is rarely symmetric. Times have a floor and no ceiling. Match lengths have a ceiling set by the timer. Ratings bunch against the ends of the scale. Expect skew and check for it, rather than assuming the bell shape from school statistics.

title: Distributions and Variation
text:
Outliers
An outlier is a value far from the rest. The boxplot’s convention is any point more than one and a half box-widths beyond the edge of the box, and R draws those points individually. That rule is a prompt to look, not a verdict.
An outlier is one of three things, and the response to each is different:








The outlier is
Example
What you do




An error
A session length of −3 minutes; a rating of 7 on a 1–5 scale
Fix it or remove it, and record that you did


An extreme but ordinary player
One tester who never died
Keep it; report the median rather than the mean


The finding
A cluster of games that collapse early
Keep it and investigate it; it is why you ran the test



Never delete an outlier because it is inconvenient. Every row you drop is a decision with a consequence (rule 6), and the value most tempting to drop is often the one the playtest was run to find (rule 9).

title: Distributions and Variation
text:
Reading Several Summaries Together
No single statistic describes a distribution, but a small set of them, read together, usually does.








Summary
What it tells you
What it misses




Mean
The total spread evenly across players
Skew, clusters, tails


Median
The middle player
How extreme the extremes are


Standard deviation
Typical distance from the mean
Which direction the spread goes


IQR
Width of the middle half
Everything outside the middle half


95th or 99th percentile
How bad the worst few per cent get
The typical case



Where the summaries disagree, look at the picture. Mean and median apart means skew. A large standard deviation with a small IQR means a few extreme values. A normal median with a bad 99th percentile means a rare problem that the average will never show. Each disagreement is a pointer to a specific shape, and the histogram confirms which one (rule 4).

title: Distributions and Variation
text:
Worked Examples
Which build runs better? The Tidebreak team captured 4500 frames from each build, split across 3 level zones. The frame-rate counter reports Build A at 58.8 FPS and Build B at 59 FPS. By the number everyone quotes, Build B is marginally the faster build.
The median agrees: 16.99 ms per frame for Build A, 16.63 ms for Build B. So does the 95th percentile: 18.8 ms against 18.4 ms. Three summaries, one verdict.
The 99th percentile disagrees. Build A’s is 19.5 ms; Build B’s is 39.4 ms, 2.0 times as long. The standard deviation says the same thing more quietly: 1.05 ms for Build A, 3.4 ms for Build B.
Count the frames slower than 30 FPS (33.3 ms). Build A has 0. Build B has 60, every one of them in the Corridor zone, and exactly 25 frames apart: at 60 FPS, a hitch 2.4 times a second for as long as the player is in the corridor.

corridor_a <- frames$ms[frames$build == "A" & frames$zone == "Corridor"]

plot(corridor_b[1:200], type = "l", col = "firebrick",
     ylim = c(10, 65),
     main = "Corridor frame times, first 200 frames",
     xlab = "Frame", ylab = "Frame time (ms)")
lines(corridor_a[1:200], col = "grey40")
abline(h = 1000 / 60, lty = 2)
legend("top", legend = c("Build A", "Build B"), horiz = TRUE,
       col = c("grey40", "firebrick"), lty = 1, bty = "n")








Why the mean cannot see it. The slow frames are 1.3% of Build B’s total. Spread across every frame of the capture, they barely move the mean, and Build B’s faster frames elsewhere more than make up for them. The 95th percentile sits below the problem because the problem is rarer than one frame in twenty. Only a summary aimed at the worst one per cent can see it, which is why the 99th percentile is the standard figure in performance capture. The mean is not approximately wrong here. It is structurally incapable of showing the thing players experience.

title: Distributions and Variation
text:
R Demonstrations
Base R first, then the tidyverse equivalent for the grouped summary.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)

sessions <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_sessions.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
frames   <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_frame_times.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)


hist(sessions$session_minutes, breaks = 20,
     main = "Session length", xlab = "Minutes",
     col = "grey85", border = "white")








hist() draws the distribution of one numeric variable. Look for the bulk, the tails, and any second hump.

boxplot(session_minutes ~ build, data = sessions,
        main = "Session length by build", ylab = "Minutes", col = "grey85")







tapply(sessions$session_minutes, sessions$build, sd)

       A        B 
8.301448 6.942605 

tapply(sessions$session_minutes, sessions$build, IQR)

    A     B 
16.25 10.95 


boxplot() with y ~ group puts one box per group on the same axis, which is the quickest way to compare distributions. Build A’s box is wider: its IQR is 16.3 minutes against 10.9 for Build B. 88% of Build A sessions were still going at minute 11, and 68% at minute 13. The spread is where Build A loses its players.

barplot(table(sessions$quit_reason),
        main = "How sessions ended", ylab = "Sessions", col = "grey85")








barplot() draws counts of a categorical variable. Give it the output of table(), not the raw column.

plot(sessions$deaths, sessions$score,
     main = "Deaths against score", xlab = "Deaths", ylab = "Score",

title: Distributions and Variation
text:
Interpretation Guidance
What the data shows. Build A and Build B have near-identical mean frame times. Build B has 60 frames slower than 30 FPS, all in the Corridor, and Build A has 0.
What the analysis suggests. Something in Build B’s Corridor costs a frame at a fixed interval. The regular spacing points at a periodic job, such as streaming, garbage collection or a timed effect, rather than at scene complexity.
What can legitimately be concluded. Build B introduced a hitch confined to the Corridor, and a report that quotes average FPS alone would have shipped it. The cause is not established by frame times; that needs a profiler.
Quote the tail with the centre. For anything where the worst case is what players remember, such as frame time, load time or matchmaking wait, report the median and a high percentile together. “Median 16.6 ms, 99th percentile 39 ms” is a performance report. “59 FPS” is a slogan.

title: Distributions and Variation
text:
Common Mistakes
Reporting average FPS as the performance result. It is the number the engine shows and the number least able to show a hitch.
Comparing groups by their means alone. Two builds with the same mean can be different games (rule 7). Draw the boxplots side by side.
Deleting outliers to clean the chart. Find out which of the three kinds each one is first. The Sentinel’s low scores in Describing What You Have are the finding, not the noise.
Quoting a standard deviation for skewed data. It measures distance from the mean, and on skewed data the mean is in the wrong place. Use the IQR.
Stopping at the 95th percentile. A problem affecting one frame in a hundred is invisible at the 95th. Match the percentile to how rare the problem could be.
Reading a scatterplot as proof. A downward cloud of points shows that two things move together in this sample. It does not say which one causes the other.

text:
Summary

An average describes a group; it does not describe any player in it.
The standard deviation is the typical distance from the mean. Use the IQR when the data is skewed.
Skew pulls the mean towards the tail. Game data is rarely symmetric.
An outlier is an error, an extreme player or the finding. Work out which before doing anything to it.

Reflective Questions

A producer asks for “one number” to show the build’s performance has improved. Which number do you give, and what do you say about the numbers you left out?
Build A’s session lengths are more spread out than Build B’s. Is a narrower spread always better for a game? Give a case where it would not be.

The Corridor hitch affects 1.3% of Build B’s frames. At what point does a rare problem stop being worth fixing, and who should decide?

title: Ten Rules for Reading Playtest Data
text:
These ten rules are the spine of this module’s analytics strand. Each one is unpacked in the notes that follow, and every lab will send you back to at least one of them. When a lab says “rule 5 again”, this is the page it means.



Decide what would change your mind before you look at the data. An analysis that cannot come out against you is not an analysis.
A number without a question attached is decoration. Ask the question first, in words, and in the form a designer would ask it.
Know what kind of number you are holding. You cannot average a category, and a 1–5 rating is not a measurement.
Look at the shape before you quote the average. Every summary throws information away; the shape tells you what was thrown.
The mean is the wrong summary more often than you think. Anything skewed — completion times, session lengths, frame times — belongs to the median.
Cleaning is analysis. Every row you drop is a decision with a consequence, and you must be able to say what it was.
Compare distributions, not averages. Two groups with the same mean can be completely different games.
Small samples lie confidently. Report how many people you measured, every time, in the same breath as the result.
Sometimes the rare value is the whole story. Averages hide stutter, crashes, and the one puzzle where everybody quits.
A finding that does not name an action is not finished. What => Pattern => Meaning => Action.

title: Why Developers Measure Anything
text: The first notes page of the strand, for everyone, before Lab 01. It sets out when measurement is worth the effort, where playtest data comes from, and how to turn a designer’s question into something you can record. The only code is in the R Demonstrations section near the end.

title: Why Developers Measure Anything
Why Developers Measure Anything
text:
Why This Matters for Playtesting
Every team makes decisions about their game constantly. Most of those decisions are made from memory, taste and the loudest voice in the room, and most of the time that is fine — taste is why anyone plays your game rather than a spreadsheet.
Measurement earns its place in the cases where taste reliably fails. There are three of them, and they recur in every project.
You cannot see your own game any more. You have played your level five hundred times. You know where the key is. You cannot un-know it, and no amount of care will let you experience your own tutorial as a stranger. This is the single most common cause of a game that the team finds obvious and the player finds impenetrable.
You cannot feel a rare event. A stutter that happens once every two seconds occupies less than one per cent of frames. Your average frame rate will not show it. Your players will talk about nothing else.
You cannot remember twenty playtests. After a session you remember the two people who struggled most and the last person you watched. You do not remember the distribution, and you will confidently reconstruct one that never existed.

title: Why Developers Measure Anything
text:
The Three Sources
Almost everything you will analyse in a game project comes from one of three places, and they have very different characters.
Telemetry is what the game records about itself while it runs: positions, events, deaths, times, item pickups. It is objective, it arrives in enormous quantities, and it tells you what happened and never why. Telemetry is cheap to collect and easy to collect badly — a log with no session identifier or no timestamp is close to worthless.
Performance capture is a special case of telemetry with its own conventions and its own failure modes. Frame times, memory, draw calls. It is the one area where the standard summary — average frame rate — is actively misleading, which is why Section 5 spends its time there.
Asking people is surveys, interviews and think-aloud sessions. It is the only source that tells you why, and the least reliable. People misremember, they are polite, they rationalise, and they answer the question they think you meant. A survey tells you what a player believes about their experience, which is a real and useful thing, but it is not the same as what happened.
The three disagree, and that is the point. The most valuable finding in any playtest is usually the place where telemetry and opinion contradict each other: players say the level is fine and the heat map shows nobody finds the side route; players say the game runs smoothly and the frame log shows a hitch every two seconds. A team with only one source never finds these.

title: Why Developers Measure Anything
section: Turning a Vague Question into a Measurable One
text:
Turning a Vague Question into a Measurable One
The question a designer asks is almost never answerable as asked.







What you are asked
What you can actually measure




“Is the level too hard?”
Deaths per attempt; time to first completion; proportion who never finish; where attempts end


“Does the game feel good?”
Time to first successful interaction; retry rate after failure; rated responsiveness


“Is the tutorial working?”
Proportion who use the taught mechanic later, unprompted


“Do people like the art?”
Rated appeal; which screenshots they choose; where they stop to look



Notice that each right-hand cell names a specific number you could write down after watching one person play. That is the test. If you cannot describe how you would record it for a single player, you have not finished turning the question into a measurement.
Notice also that the right-hand column is often not one measure but several, and that they can disagree. This is not a failure of the method. A tutorial that everybody completes and nobody learns from is a real and common outcome, and only two measures together can find it.

title: Why Developers Measure Anything
text:
Deciding in Advance
Before you collect anything, write down what result would change your mind. “If more than a third of testers never find the second key, I will add a light cue.”
This costs nothing and protects you from the most comfortable mistake in the discipline: running the test, getting an ambiguous result, and finding in it whatever you already believed. If the threshold is written down beforehand, the data gets to answer. If it is not, you will answer and attribute it to the data.

title: Why Developers Measure Anything
text:
Worked Examples
The question as asked. The Tidebreak team ran 120 playtest sessions, 60 on Build A and 60 on Build B. The designer’s question is “is Build A worse?”, which cannot be answered as asked: worse at what, for whom, by how much?
The question as measured. Two measures bear on it, one from each end of the three sources:








Source
Measure
Recorded per player as




Telemetry
Did the session end in a frustration quit?
quit_reason is Frustrated


Asking people
“I always knew what my objective was”
A rating from 1 to 5



The threshold, written first. Before anyone opens the file, the team writes: “If more than a quarter of the sessions on either build end in a frustration quit, that build does not ship.”
The result. 20 of 60 Build A sessions ended in a frustration quit (33%), against 5 of 60 on Build B (8%). Build A crosses the line; Build B does not. Nobody has to argue about it, because the argument happened before the data arrived.
The second source. Of the 8 survey items, the objective item is the lowest rated, with a mean of 2.61 on the 1 to 5 scale. Telemetry says what happened: players on Build A left in frustration. The survey offers a candidate for why: players did not know what they were meant to be doing. Neither source alone would have pointed a designer at the objective marker.

title: Why Developers Measure Anything
text:
Interpretation Guidance
Every finding is read at three levels, and the discipline is keeping them apart.
What the data shows. 20 of 60 Build A sessions ended in a frustration quit, against 5 of 60 on Build B. This is a count. It is not in dispute.
What the analysis suggests. Something in Build A frustrates players that Build B avoided, and the survey’s weakest item points at objective clarity as a candidate.
What can legitimately be concluded. Build A fails the threshold the team set in advance. That is all. The survey figure is averaged across both builds, so on its own it cannot say that the unclear objective belongs to Build A. Linking the two is a hypothesis for the next test, not a finding.
Telemetry reports behaviour and surveys report belief. When they agree, you have a lead. When they disagree, you have the most valuable finding in the playtest, and the disagreement itself is what goes in the report.

title: Why Developers Measure Anything
text:
Common Mistakes
Collecting first, asking later. Logging everything and hoping a question emerges produces large files and no decisions. Write the question down first (rule 2).
Trusting one source. A survey on its own tells you what players believe; a log on its own tells you what they did. Treat either alone as half the evidence.
Setting the threshold after seeing the result. A threshold chosen after the data has been seen is always met by exactly the right margin. If it was not written down beforehand, it is not a threshold (rule 1).
Logging without identifiers. A death event with no session or player ID cannot be joined to anything, and a survey response with no session ID cannot be joined to the telemetry from the same match.
Reading glimpse() and moving on. The types it prints are R’s guess. A 1 to 5 rating arrives as <dbl>, and R will average it without complaint. Whether it should be averaged is a decision R cannot make for you.

title: Why Developers Measure Anything
text:
Summary

Measurement earns its place where taste fails: you cannot see your own game, feel a rare event, or remember twenty playtests.
Telemetry says what happened, performance capture says how the machine coped, and asking people says what players believe. The disagreements are the findings.
A question is measurable when you can say how you would record it for one player.
Write the threshold that would change your mind before you look.

ggplot(sessions, aes(x = wrong_turns)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "grey60") +
  facet_grid(cohort ~ build)
